# Selecting the Best Few with Human Evaluators: Adaptively Combining Ratings and Pairwise Comparisons **Abstract.** This paper considers a decision-maker tasked with identifying the _k_ best items from a large pool of candidates, such as job applicants, LLMs, award nominees, or new product ideas. The decision-maker learns about the items’ quality by soliciting human evaluations. Each evaluation can be costly, so the decision-maker aims to use the limited evaluation budget efficiently by allocating evaluations adaptively. A key consideration is the form of evaluation to solicit, which should be something evaluators are comfortable providing. Two popular forms are ratings and pairwise comparisons, and we allow for both, as they may be especially useful in combination given the limited budget. Ratings can be used early on to get a coarse picture of which items are good and which are not. As that picture forms, comparisons can refine the ordering of the good items, narrowing in on the ultimate top-_k_ selection. To solve the allocation problem, we develop an adaptive algorithm built from two allocation policies. The first, our primary contribution, is based on a surrogate objective that is naturally forward-looking, valuing evaluations that help inform what to evaluate in future rounds, not just those that directly improve the selection decision. The decision rule is interpretable, and we prove that it is asymptotically consistent. Late in the evaluation process, when being forward-looking is less productive, we construct a myopic policy and a criterion for switching to it. In simulation, the method gives insight into how to combine these two types of evaluations, and beats the (limited) existing benchmarks. **Key words:** ranking and selection, top-_k_ identification, pairwise comparisons, ratings, human evaluations ### 1. Introduction This paper considers a decision-maker tasked with identifying the _k_ best items from a large pool of candidates. This is done using data the decision-maker sources sequentially from human evaluators, where the adaptive choice of upcoming evaluations is informed by what has been learned so far. When modeling such human judgment, a key decision is the form of the evaluation input. While one may wish for some sophisticated multidimensional input, providing it is often beyond the scope, time, and ability for evaluators, which is why inputs such as thumbs-up/thumbs-down and swiping left or right have become popular. Rather than restrict the decision-maker to soliciting one type of input, we allow for the combination of thumbs-up/thumbs-down ratings and pairwise comparisons, which, as we will discuss, can be complementary in our problem. This model can form a basis for many applications, including selecting the best few among LLMs, job applicants, university applicants, financial analysts, award nominees, promotion candidates, new product ideas, and sports draft prospects. While problems of this type are clearly important, they also tend to be difficult in two distinct ways. One challenge is the _analysis and algorithm design_. The aim is a sequential evaluation allocation policy that is Motti Goldberger

<tbc>both close to optimal and structured enough to yield insight and earn practitioners’ trust. The other difficulty is the _modeling_, which connects the application to the analysis and sets the stage for how useful that analysis will be. First, we position the problem in the literature and walk through the modeling decisions involved. We then discuss how we arrived at our solution approach.

The problem of identifying the best few items by allocating evaluation resources is central to the _ranking and selection_ and _best-arm identification_ literatures, where what we refer to as evaluations are typically called samples. Unlike the classical work on multi-armed bandits (Robbins 1952), where rewards are collected while learning, here the only concern is with the quality of the terminal selection, the setting known as _pure exploration_ (Bubeck et al. 2009). Much of this literature focuses on identifying the best (top-1) item (Chen et al. 2000, Frazier et al. 2008, Chen and Ryzhov 2023). We consider the more general problem of top-_k_ identification (Chen et al. 2008, Zhang et al. 2023, Liu et al. 2024).

In this literature, evaluating (sampling) an item typically means directly observing a noisy realization of its utility (quality), which we will refer to as untransformed evaluations. Such untransformed input is natural in applications such as simulation optimization and hyperparameter tuning, where the observed output is itself the object being optimized. In our setting, the utility of each item is latent, since the value of including each item in the chosen set is never evaluated directly. Instead, each item’s quality is observed indirectly through evaluations that take the form of ratings or pairwise comparisons, both of which transform the latent utilities into coarse ordinal outcomes.

To highlight why we do not rely on adapting an established algorithm, we highlight three common modeling and analysis decisions in the ranking and selection literature. We discuss how each decision relates to our problem and, when relevant, how we overcome the additional challenges posed by differences in our setting.

The first modeling decision concerns the terminal objective: how we grade an evaluation allocation policy based on the _k_ items it ultimately selects. The two most common choices are the probability of correct selection (PCS) (Chen et al. 2000, Glynn and Juneja 2004, Li et al. 2025) and the expected opportunity cost (EOC) (Chick and Inoue 2001, Chick et al. 2010, Gao and Chen 2015a). PCS is the probability that the selected set is exactly the true top-_k_, so it treats every incorrect selection equally. EOC is the expected shortfall in utility between the selected set and the true top-_k_ set, making bigger selection mistakes more costly. PCS suits highly specialized or high-stakes decisions where any deviation from the best possible selection is considered a failure. For more common tasks, where a serious mistake can be far costlier than a marginal one, EOC can be the more natural fit. Since EOC is more aligned with the applications we consider, we adopt it in this work.

A second decision concerns how the allocation problem is formulated, with two common formulations at opposite ends of the spectrum. One is static allocation, where the decision variable is the total number of evaluations assigned to each item. The other is dynamic learning, where evaluations are chosen one at a time and each outcome is observed before the next evaluation is chosen. In the static formulation, writing<tbc>

<tbc>**_N_**=(_N_<sub>1</sub>_,...,N<sub>I</sub>_) for the vector of evaluations assigned to items _i_=1_,...,I_ and _R_ for the total evaluation budget, the allocation problem is

\(min_N\text{EOC}(N)\text{s.t.}\sum_{i=1}^IN_i\le R.\)

This allocation problem faces two main difficulties. The objective EOC(**_N_**), and likewise PCS(**_N_**), generally does not have a closed form that is amenable to analysis. Additionally, the problem is an integer program, which typically makes it intractable to consider the full solution space at scale. In the fully dynamic formulation, one evaluation is chosen at a time, avoiding the combinatorial complexity of the static problem. At each decision point, the state consists of the current posterior distribution over the items’ utilities and the remaining budget, and the action is the next evaluation. The state transition updates the posterior based on the outcome and deducts the evaluation’s cost from the remaining budget. This problem is formulated as a dynamic program which is intractable because the combination of possible evaluations, outcomes, transitions, and future states grows rapidly with the horizon (Frazier et al. 2008, Hong et al. 2021, Zhang et al. 2023).

Our base formulation is fully dynamic with evaluations chosen sequentially. However, allocating one evaluation at a time can have logistical obstacles. There may be considerable overhead in assigning and conducting evaluations, which can favor giving an evaluator a _batch_ of tasks at once. We therefore also consider a hybrid approach in §6, where a batch of evaluations is chosen in each round. This sits between the two formulations and inherits both difficulties. Within a round, the allocation is an integer program, each linked through the between-round dynamics.

The complexity of the problem under both formulations has given rise to a variety of solution approaches. Before turning to our own, we discuss the three most relevant well-studied families, all developed in the untransformed evaluation setting. The first is a family of algorithms known as Optimal Computing Budget Allocation (OCBA), originating with Chen et al. (1997, 2000), Glynn and Juneja (2004). At a high level, the algorithm loops through three steps: (i) take the items’ current mean estimates as if they were the ground truth utilities, (ii) choose the next evaluation(s) by determining the static allocation that would maximize PCS (or minimize EOC), and (iii) update the estimates of the means based on the outcome. However, step (ii) is intractable due to the complexities of the static allocation problem discussed above. To overcome this, it is common to consider the asymptotic regime where \(R\rightarrow\infty\) and find the allocation proportions that (approximately) optimize the resulting problem. Eventually, the estimated means will converge to the true means, and thus the evaluation proportions will converge to the (approximately) optimal proportions. The majority of the OCBA literature studies the top-1 setting with PCS, with extensions to top-1 EOC (He et al. 2007, Gao et al. 2017), as well as to top-_k_ PCS (Chen et al. 2008, Gao and Chen 2015b, Zhang et al. 2016) and top-_k_ EOC (Gao and Chen 2015a). Such approaches tend to perform better in large-budget settings. In fact, for small budgets, it has been demonstrated that such allocation procedures may even perform worse than equal allocation (Peng et al. 2018, Liu et al. 2024).

<tbc>A second family of algorithms considers the dynamic formulation restricted to one-step look-ahead policies, see Powell and Ryzhov (2012) for an overview. At each round, the decision-maker chooses the evaluation that (approximately) maximizes the expected value of information (EVI), the improvement in the quality of the terminal selection that results from one additional evaluation. For top-1 identification, Chick and Inoue (2001), Chick et al. (2010) derive policies that approximately maximize EVI for both the PCS and EOC objectives. Recently, Zhang et al. (2023) developed a top-_k_ identification policy that maximizes an approximation of the EVI for PCS. Assuming evaluations follow Gaussian distributions with known variances, Frazier et al. (2008) derive the exact one-step look-ahead policy that maximizes the EVI for EOC, known as the knowledge gradient (KG) policy. In our setting, however, KG’s myopia can be particularly detrimental with binary evaluations (Groves and Branke 2019, Li et al. 2024). We return to this point in §2.3.

A third related family of algorithms is based on the expected improvement (EI) approach (Jones et al. 1998), which originated in the Bayesian Optimization literature. Various works have studied its application to top-1 identification (Ryzhov 2016, Qin et al. 2017, Chen and Ryzhov 2019). In its simplest form, EI scores each item by how much its utility, in expectation, exceeds that of the current best candidate and evaluates the item with the highest score. EI’s simplicity is appealing, and although it does not explicitly look ahead, it still reflects future dynamics: evaluating items with high potential to improve on the current best can help inform which evaluations to conduct in future rounds. However, EI does not naturally extend to reflect alternative evaluation forms with different information contents and costs. Furthermore, it chooses which _single_ item to evaluate next, whereas our evaluation alternatives include choosing a _pair_ to compare.

Finally, the third modeling decision concerns the form of the evaluations themselves. In psychometrics, the field of measurement of psychological data, the two most common forms of input for human feedback are ratings, where an evaluation assigns a categorical score to a particular item, and rankings, where a set of items is ordered relative to one another (Thurstone 1927, Likert 1932, Torgerson 1958). We consider each in its parsimonious form--binary thumbs-up/thumbs-down ratings and pairwise comparisons--both among the most common input choices. Restricting to these simple versions of ordinal feedback keeps evaluators’ cognitive load low (Revilla et al. 2014, Kutscher and Eid 2024). The two input forms have distinct pros and cons in our setting. Ratings can be cheaper and easier to provide than pairwise comparisons (White et al. 2024), and a few of them can be an efficient way to establish the ballpark utility of an item. However, ratings are not efficient at distinguishing the relative order of close items, which is essential for differentiating between top-_k_ candidates. Additionally, a rating (say, a thumbs-up) can carry a different meaning to different evaluators, resulting in potential ambiguity when aggregating and interpreting them. Pairwise comparisons, in contrast, only contain _relative_ information about item utilities, and while their interpretation is unambiguous, their usefulness depends heavily on which items are paired. The number of possible pairings is quadratic in the number of items, so starting from an uninformed prior would result in many unhelpful pairings early on. For example, we might compare the items that turn out to be the two worst. Even if that comparison<tbc>

<tbc>provides a strong signal about which of the two is better, it does little to inform us about which items are in the top-_k_. However, once we do have a clear sense of which items are top-_k_ contenders, comparisons can be far more effective than ratings at pinning down their relative ordering (Li et al. 2018). It follows that the two evaluation forms can be especially useful when combined (Fageot et al. 2026). Intuitively, ratings can be used more in early rounds to get a coarse picture of which items are "good" and which are not, and then as that picture forms, comparisons can gradually take over, refining the relative ordering of the good items and narrowing in on the ultimate top-_k_ selection. Our model allows the two evaluation types to differ in accuracy and cost (effort), following the empirical findings of Pérez-Ortiz et al. (2020) and White et al. (2024).

The two evaluation forms can also interact in non-intuitive ways. Consider a simple example with four items, _A_, _B_, _C_, and _D_, whose utilities are independent ex-ante. With ratings alone, a rating of _B_ informs its utility relative to the other items but leaves our beliefs about their utilities unchanged. Now suppose we observe the comparisons \(A\succ B\) and \(C\succ D\), followed by \(B\succ C\). Intuitively, the third comparison suggests that _A_ is preferred to _D_ even though neither was involved in the comparison. The mechanism by which our model reflects this is that comparisons create dependency in the joint posterior over the utilities: the third comparison raises _B_’s estimate and thereby also lifts _A_, while lowering _C_’s estimate and thereby also lowering _D_. This dependency also changes what we learn from a rating. A subsequent rating of _B_ can now influence our posterior beliefs about _A_, _C_, and _D_. In fact, with a more complex comparison history, a rating of _B_ can even reverse our estimated relative ranking of two non-evaluated items, such as _A_ and _D_. Thus, the value of an evaluation for informing the top-_k_ set may not be apparent from what it tells us about the evaluated items alone. Including such dependency in the joint posterior is an opportunity, as it leads to better discrimination between items and hence a more accurate top-_k_ choice. But this added accuracy does not come for free: reflecting the dependency in the dynamic choice of evaluations adds complexity.

Work related to top-_k_ selection tasks in which evaluations are, like ours, binary pairwise comparisons (and possibly also ratings) is scarce in the literature, especially with small budgets. In this setting, one common approach to model evaluations is to assign each possible _evaluation_ its own parameter. For pairwise comparisons, this means a separate parameter specification for each pair of items, representing the probability that one item is preferred to the other. Although the outcomes are binary, this model is still in the untransformed evaluation setting: the outcomes remain a direct noisy realization of the underlying parameter. An alternative approach is the latent-utility model of our setting, where each _item_ has a single value, its utility, that generates the comparisons (and ratings).

In the ranking and selection literature, Priekule and Meisel (2017), Groves and Branke (2019), Li et al. (2024) study top-1 and top-_k_ selection with binary pairwise comparisons under the first evaluation model. Their methodology does not transfer to our problem, as their more flexible model requires learning the parameters of _I(I_-1)/2 item pairs, which is unrealistic in small-budget settings. More fundamentally, they<tbc>

<tbc>only consider pairwise comparisons, and it is not clear how one could combine ratings and comparisons under this model.

In the crowdsourcing literature, these problems are more commonly studied under latent-utility models. Chen et al. (2016) develop an approximate KG algorithm for learning the full ranking of items (as opposed to the top-_k_) from pairwise comparisons. Li et al. (2018), Pérez-Ortiz et al. (2020), Fageot et al. (2026) develop a unified statistical model for combining pairwise comparisons and ratings. Fageot et al. (2026) show empirically that combining ratings and pairwise comparisons can improve estimation of the latent utilities. More directly related to our problem, Li et al. (2018) also give a heuristic approach for choosing evaluations for top-_k_ selection, a slightly modified version of which we use as a benchmark.

Finally, top-_k_ identification from pairwise comparisons is well studied in the dueling-bandit and active- ranking literature. Usually set in the fixed-confidence regime where sampling continues until a target confidence is reached (as opposed to a fixed budget _R_), these algorithms tend to require large numbers of evaluations--far beyond the budgets we consider. See, e.g., Mohajer et al. (2017), Ren et al. (2018), Chen et al. (2018), Heckel et al. (2019), Saha and Gopalan (2019), Ren et al. (2020), Saha and Gopalan (2020), Goldberger and Rudi (2026a) for recent developments and Bengs et al. (2021) for a review.

Instead of explaining our evaluation allocation approach directly, we find it easier to lay out where it came from. Our starting point was the KG policy primarily because, among the existing methods, it is well suited for small-budget problems and can naturally accommodate the combination of evaluation types--our key initial motivation for undertaking this research. However, the KG policy allocates evaluations in each round as if the final selection would immediately follow. Except for the last evaluation, that is not the actual task. The task is to prepare for the terminal selection, and it may be that the best evaluation to do next is decided by how it may inform later evaluation choices. To illustrate how much KG misses out on future dynamics, consider that in its eyes any evaluation whose outcome cannot change the current top-_k_ set has no value at all.

Ideally, we would incorporate the full dynamics into the evaluation choices, but based on the existing literature, anything beyond solving a sequence of state-dependent, static problems seems out of reach. Our key insight leading to our approach came from flipping the perspective from the positive focus on what the decision-maker wants to achieve--choosing the best _k_ items--to a negative perspective--how to reduce errors. There are two ways to err ex-post: including an item that does not belong (_inclusion error_) and excluding one that does (_exclusion error_). Ex-ante, items have an expected _mismatch loss_: the expected magnitude of an inclusion error for items in the current top-_k_ and an exclusion error for those not in it. We then construct a per-round _surrogate_ objective that values uncertainty reduction by how much it reduces the expected mismatch loss. We contrast this with the KG policy that adopts the terminal top-_k_ EOC as each round’s objective. It uses the current uncertainty to assess possible changes in the membership of the top-_k posterior means_. Our method instead holds the current means fixed and values an evaluation by how much it is expected to reduce _uncertainty_. The terminal top-_k_ decision then drives the evaluation choices<tbc>

<tbc>only implicitly by providing a measure of where uncertainty reduction is more valuable. This surrogate is naturally forward-looking. It seeks to reduce uncertainty about the items currently near the top-_k_ cutoff without requiring any direct change to the current top-_k_ set. Doing so pays off in future rounds, since the more effective we are at singling out items near the top-_k_ cutoff, the more effectively we can direct the remaining evaluations.

The difficulty is that mismatch loss does not admit an analysis-friendly expression. The magnitude of an item’s error depends on where it stands relative to the _k_th or (_k_+1)th best of the remaining items, so computing an item’s mismatch loss requires an expectation with respect to the joint utility distribution and an order statistic of the other _I_-1 items, where even the latter itself is intractable. Our resolution is to replace this random top-_k_ threshold with a simpler threshold that is recalibrated each round, such that, in expectation, _k_ items’ utilities will exceed it. With this threshold, an item’s mismatch loss depends only on the marginal distribution of its utility relative to it. This separability gives a clean and interpretable way to account for an evaluation’s effect on _all_ items, those being directly evaluated and, via covariance, those that are not. The sum of these mismatch losses is our surrogate objective, and in each round, the policy chooses the evaluation whose reduction of this loss per evaluation cost is largest.

We also point out a potential trap that arises when combining the two evaluation types, in part because we initially fell into it. Ratings contain information about the average utility of the items, while comparisons do not. Learning about this average reduces the variance of each item’s utility but does not help distinguish the top-_k_, since shifting all utilities together leaves their ordering unchanged. A surrogate that rewards this reduction in variance would therefore unfairly favor ratings over comparisons. We discuss this issue in §3 and show that our surrogate does not reward learning about the average utility, so ratings and comparisons are on equal footing.

As the horizon approaches its end, being forward-looking becomes less valuable, and this strength of the surrogate can become a weakness. In this regime, the myopia of the KG policy would be desirable. We therefore develop the KG policy for our problem, with a switching criterion for the _endgame_, the final rounds where its myopia outperforms the surrogate.

We support our method through both analysis and simulation. In the analysis, although the surrogate objective was constructed from analytical intuition rather than derived, we show that it can be obtained from an upper bound on the EOC, which rigorously justifies and refines our choice of the top-_k_ threshold. We also prove that the resulting policy that allocates by minimizing the surrogate in each round is asymptotically consistent. In simulation, we show that the allocations this policy produces are intuitive and insightful, and that it substantially outperforms existing benchmarks.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: §2 presents the model and defines the objective. §3 develops the surrogate objective, which §4 uses to construct the sequential evaluation procedure and establish its asymptotic consistency. §5 develops the knowledge gradient policy for the endgame and the switching rule.

<tbc>§6 considers the batch setting. §7 reports the results of the numerical experiments, and §8 gives concluding remarks.

## 2. Model and objective

This section defines the generative data model for pairwise comparisons and ratings, introduces the sequential evaluation process and formulates the optimization problem as a dynamic program. We then demonstrate that the KG policy is not well-suited for our setting, which motivates the surrogate objective of §3.

### 2.1. Generative model

We consider **_I_** items with latent utilities \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_I)\in\mathbb{R}^I\), which represent the values of selecting each item. We adopt a Bayesian framework and place a Gaussian prior on the utility vector, \(\theta\sim N(\mu_0,\Sigma_0)\) where \(\Sigma_0\) is positive definite. When preliminary information distinguishes the items, \(\mu_0\) and \(\Sigma_0\) can reflect it. When no such information is available, or when items are people and a prior that discriminates raises ethical or legal concerns, an exchangeable prior (\(\mu_0=\mathbf{0}\), \(\Sigma_0=s\mathrm{Id}_I\)) treats all items symmetrically.

Evaluators can provide two types of feedback, _pairwise comparisons_ and _ratings_. A _pairwise comparison_ of items _i_ and _j_ produces a binary outcome: one item is preferred to the other. The event that an evaluator prefers _i_ to _j_ is denoted by \(i\succ j\), and its probability is determined by \(\theta_i-\theta_j+\epsilon_1\), where \(\epsilon_1\sim N(0,\sigma_1^2)\). Thus, the evaluator’s ability to distinguish between the two items depends on the difference in their utilities and on \(\epsilon_1\), which captures imperfections in pairwise evaluations. The subscript 1 is used because item _i_ is compared to 1 other item. A _rating_ of item _i_ produces a binary ‘thumbs-up’ or ‘thumbs-down’ outcome, where item _i_ is implicitly compared to some utility threshold \(\theta_0\). Note that \(\theta_0\) is not a part of \(\theta\)--we use this notation to facilitate unified expressions for pairwise comparisons and ratings. Similar to the pairwise comparison model, the event that an evaluator ranks _i_ above the threshold is denoted by \(i\succ 0\) and its probability is determined by \(\theta_i-\theta_0+\epsilon_0\), where \(\epsilon_0\sim N(0,\sigma_0^2)\). Here \(\epsilon_0\) captures two sources of noise: the evaluator’s ability to estimate item _i_’s utility and the uncertainty about where the latent threshold \(\theta_0\) lies. The subscript 0 is used because item _i_ is compared to 0 items.

The set of possible evaluations is given by \(\mathcal{I}:=\left\{(i,j):0\le j<i\le I\right\}.\) Define _j_=min(_j,_1), which is 0(1) when an evaluation is a rating (comparison). For an evaluation \((i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\), let _X<sub>ij</sub>_ denote the outcome where<tbc>

\(X_{ij}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
1 & \text{if}i\succ j \\
-1 & \text{if}i\prec j,
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>and, conditioned on the evaluator-noise term \(\epsilon_J\), \(\mathbb{P}(X_{ij}=1|\theta,\epsilon_J)=g(\theta_i-\theta_j+\epsilon_J)\), where \(g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow(0,1)\) is some link function. For the remainder of the paper, unless specified otherwise, we consider the probit link function, commonly used to model human ordinal rating data (Liddell and Kruschke 2018), i.e., \(g=\Phi\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF and \(\phi\) its density. Thus,

\(\mathbb{P}(X_{ij}=1|\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon_J}\left[\Phi\left(\theta_i-\theta_j+\epsilon_J\right)\right]=\Phi\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\sigma_J^2}}(\theta_i-\theta_j)\right)=\Phi\left(\beta_J(\theta_i-\theta_j)\right),\)

<tbc>where \(\beta_j:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\sigma_j^2}}\in(0,1]\), for \(j\in\{0,1\}\), captures the evaluator precision when providing a rating or a pairwise comparison. As shown in Pérez-Ortiz et al. (2020), a single latent-utility model for ratings and pairwise comparisons can fit human data well as long as the two evaluation types are allowed to differ in signal quality, which we capture through \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). In addition to variation in signal quality, there may also be heterogeneity in evaluator accuracy and bias. If these differences were known, our model would capture this by using different values of \(\theta_0\), \(\beta_0\), and \(\beta_1\) for each evaluator. Because they are generally unknown, we instead use common parameters across evaluators, effectively absorbing evaluator-level variation into the noise terms rather than learning evaluator-specific accuracy or bias from past evaluations. This is a standard simplification in the literature, and models using it have been shown to still fit human data well (Pérez-Ortiz et al. 2020). Learning evaluator-specific parameters could further inform the allocation, but would introduce an additional inference problem that we leave for future work. In the numerical experiments of §7, we stress-test this assumption by using synthetic data where accuracy and bias differ across evaluators.

One may question the feasibility of calibrating these parameters in practice. Remark 1 shows that after fixing one for identification, the rest can be calibrated from three simple, interpretable quantities.

REMARK 1. _The binary data alone cannot identify the latent utility scale and the observation accuracy parameters simultaneously: for any c\>_0_, replacing_ \((\theta,\theta_0,\beta_0,\beta_1)\) _with_ \((c\theta,c\theta_0,\beta_0/c,\beta_1/c)\) _leaves every outcome probability_ \(\Phi\big(\beta_j(\theta_i-\theta_j)\big)\) _unchanged. Thus, one parameter can (and must) be fixed, and we fix the scale of_ \(\theta\) _by choosing the prior variance s. The remaining parameters_ \(\beta_1,\beta_0,\theta_0\) _can then be found given the following more interpretable quantities, which we formally derive in the Appendix:_

(_i)_ _The probability that a comparison of two randomly chosen items agrees with the true ordering,_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{\pi}arcsin\left(\frac{\beta_1\sqrt{2s}}{\sqrt{1+2s\beta_1^2}}\right),\)<tbc>

<tbc>_which determines_ \(\beta_1\).<tbc>

(_ii)_ _The probability that a rating of a randomly chosen item is correct,_<tbc>

<tbc>\(1-\Phi\big(\frac{\theta_0}{\sqrt{s}}\big)-\Phi\big(\frac{\beta_0\theta_0}{\sqrt{1+s\beta_0^2}}\big)+2\Phi_2\big(\frac{\theta_0}{\sqrt{s}},\frac{\beta_0\theta_0}{\sqrt{1+s\beta_0^2}};\frac{\beta_0\sqrt{s}}{\sqrt{1+s\beta_0^2}}\big),\)<tbc>

<tbc>_where_ \(\Phi_2(\cdot,\cdot;\rho)\) _is the standard bivariate normal CDF with correlation_ \(\rho\).<tbc>

(_iii)_ _The expected proportion of items that receive a ‘thumbs-up’ rating,_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\Phi\big(-\frac{\beta_0\theta_0}{\sqrt{1+s\beta_0^2}}\big),\)<tbc>

<tbc>_which together with (ii) jointly determines_ \(\beta_0\) _and_ \(\theta_0\).<tbc>

## 2.2. Sequential evaluation process

Building on the generative model, we next describe how the sequential decision process unfolds. In each round _t_=1,2_,..._, the decision-maker chooses an evaluation \((i_t,j_t)\in\mathcal{I}\), a rating or a pairwise comparison, and observes its outcome \(X_t\in\{-1,1\}\) before choosing the next evaluation. Let _r_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0 and _r_<sub>1</sub>_\>_0 be the per-evaluation resource cost of ratings and comparisons, respectively, where the resource could be monetary or capacity (time it takes to conduct an evaluation). Let _R_ denote the total evaluation budget and _R<sub>t</sub>_ the budget left at the start of round _t_, so _R_<sub>1</sub>=_R_. An evaluation (_i,j_) is affordable in round _t_ when \(r_j\le R_t\). After conducting the chosen evaluation, its cost is deducted from the remaining budget, _R_<sub>_t_+1</sub>=_R<sub>t</sub>-r<sub>j<sub>t</sub></sub>_, where _j<sub>t</sub>_=min(_j<sub>t</sub>,_1). The process continues until no evaluation is affordable. Let _T_ denote the (random) total number of evaluations conducted, so \(T:=min\{t\ge 0:R_{t+1}<min(r_0,r_1)\}\).

In round _t_, after the outcome is observed, we update the posterior according to

\(p_t(\theta)\propto p_{t-1}(\theta)\Phi\big(X_t\beta_{j_t}(\theta_{i_t}-\theta_{j_t})\big)\propto p_0(\theta)\prod_{s=1}^t\Phi\big(X_s\beta_{j_s}(\theta_{is}-\theta_{js})\big),\)

where _p_<sub>0</sub> is the prior of \(\theta\) at _t_=0. The posterior after any round _t_ is denoted by _p<sub>t</sub>_ and hence its prior is the posterior of the previous round, _p_<sub>_t_-1</sub>. Figure 1 illustrates the sequential process. Since the Gaussian prior is

not conjugate to the probit likelihood<sup>1</sup>, the posterior after each round is generally non-Gaussian. One option is to carry out posterior inference by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). ## 2.3. Shortcomings of the knowledge gradient policy

Addressing the curse of dimensionality of the dynamic program in (3), the KG policy adopts the myopic version of it, given by

\(V_\text{myopic}\big(\big((i,j)|p_{t-1}\big):=\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}}\mathbb{P}\big(X_{ij}=x\big|p_{t-1}\big)\left(\sum_{\ell\in S_k^*(\mu_t(x|(i,j)))}\mu_{t,\ell}(x|(i,j))-\sum_{\ell\in S_k^*(\mu_{t-1})}\mu_{t-1,\ell}\right).\) (4)

<tbc>The KG policy then selects an evaluation according to

\(argmax_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}:r_j\le R_t}\frac{V_\text{myopic}((i,j)|p_{t-1})}{r_J}.\)

However, binary data can cause the KG policy to get "stuck" (Li et al. 2024). If the estimated top-_k_ set is sufficiently separated from the rest, no evaluation outcome can directly change the posterior top-_k_ set because the information a single binary outcome can carry is bounded, and with it how far the posterior means can move. This can occur frequently even when the top-_k_ set is far from certain. When this happens, KG has no basis to choose among evaluations, and a fallback rule, such as random allocation, is needed. This is not an issue with unbounded observations, such as a Gaussian likelihood, where there is always a possibility that a single evaluation can provide overwhelmingly positive/negative evidence that changes the posterior top-_k_ set.

## 3. Surrogate objective

Developing the surrogate objective combines two ideas. The first is to establish the expected mismatch loss and connect it to EOC. The second is how it drives evaluation choices. We treat the expected mismatch loss as a static objective fixed at state _p_<sub>_t_-1</sub>, using it to identify where uncertainty reduction is most valuable holding the current means fixed. The remainder of this section proceeds as follows. To provide insight into how the mismatch loss was developed, §3.1 presents our initial, simpler, intuition-based version, which then leads to the formal development in §3.2 that rigorously connects the surrogate to EOC and yields an improved form. Finally, §3.3 develops the resulting surrogate loss.

### 3.1. Mismatch loss: from intuition

Recall from the introduction that mismatch loss is defined as the expected magnitude of the inclusion errors of \(S_k^*(\mu_{t-1})\) and the exclusion errors of \(\{1,\dots,I\}\backslash S_k^*(\mu_{t-1})\). Measuring the magnitude of each error requires an anchor, a top-_k_ threshold against which they are measured. However, given the prior, the number of items above a given threshold is a random variable. A natural approach is therefore to choose a threshold such that, in expectation, the number of items above it is _k_.

More explicitly, at each evaluation round _t_, fix a threshold _q_ on the utility scale such that, in expectation, _k_ items have utility above _q_ under the prior _p_<sub>_t_-1</sub>. Then for each item \(i\in S_k^*(\mu_{t-1})\) the loss is \(\mathbb{E}[(q-\theta_i)^+]\), the expected amount it falls short of the top-_k_ threshold, and similarly for each item \(i\notin S_k^*(\mu_{t-1})\) the loss is \(\mathbb{E}[(\theta_i-q)^+]\), the expected amount it exceeds the top-_k_ threshold. We refer to the sum of these losses as the (informal) _expected mismatch loss_

\(\sum_{i\in S_k^*(\mu_{t-1})}\mathbb{E}\big[(q-\theta_i)^+\big|p_{t-1}\big]+\sum_{i\notin S_k^*(\mu_{t-1})}\mathbb{E}\big[(\theta_i-q)^+\big|p_{t-1}\big].\) (5)

The policy then chooses the evaluation whose resulting uncertainty reduction on \(\theta\) reduces expected mismatch loss the most per unit of resource. Two things make this conceptually attractive. First, it naturally directs evaluations toward items near the current expected top-_k_ cutoff (_q_) and toward items with substantial prior<tbc>

<tbc>uncertainty, since those are the items that, if misclassified, will incur a high expected mismatch loss. Hence, this surrogate preserves the key feature of EOC: mistakes are penalized by their magnitude. Second, an evaluation can still be valuable even when its outcome cannot change this round’s posterior top-_k_ membership if it tightens the posterior of items near _q_. This is in part because the evaluation informs where to direct later evaluations. Attempting a sports analogy: we don’t only give credit for scoring goals but also for assists.

However, adaptively combining ratings and pairwise comparisons using this mismatch loss has a less than obvious nuance to it. Which items belong in the top-_k_ depends only on the relative utilities, not on the average utility \(\overline{\theta}\). Thus, information about a change in \(\overline{\theta}\) that shifts all utilities equally is _decision-irrelevant_, and the surrogate should catch this. However, (5) may reward learning such information, since reducing uncertainty about such a common shift reduces the expectations \(\mathbb{E}[(q-\theta_i)^+],\mathbb{E}[(\theta_i-q)^+]\). Ratings can provide information about \(\overline{\theta}\) since they contain information about an item’s absolute quality, while comparisons cannot since they only contain relative information. A surrogate based on this mismatch loss can therefore favor ratings over comparisons because it rewards decision-irrelevant uncertainty reduction.

Initially we addressed this by replacing \(\theta\) with its sum-to-zero counterpart \(\widetilde{\theta}=\theta-\overline{\theta}\mathbf{1}\), where **1** is the all-ones vector, and computing the mismatch loss based on the differences \(\widetilde{\theta}_i-q\) and \(q-\widetilde{\theta}_i\), so that learning \(\overline{\theta}\) does not affect the loss. We will next present a formal and more general treatment of mismatch loss, including its link to EOC. As a motivation for this, notice that \(\widetilde{\theta}_i-q=\theta_i-(q+\overline{\theta})\), so the mismatch loss with the fixed threshold _q_ applied to \(\widetilde{\theta}\) can be thought of as our original mismatch loss with a random \(\theta\)-dependent threshold \(q+\overline{\theta}\). This observation invites the question of what is the "best" such _random_ top-_k_ threshold that allows for tractable analysis.

## 3.2. Mismatch loss: formal derivation

We begin by formally defining mismatch loss and showing how it relates to EOC. For any utility vector \(\theta\) and any threshold function \(a:\mathbb{R}^I\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\), define the mismatch loss

\(\mathcal{M}(\theta;S_k,a):=\sum_{i\in S_k}\left(a(\theta)-\theta_i\right)^++\sum_{i\notin S_k}\left(\theta_i-a(\theta)\right)^+=ka(\theta)-\sum_{i\in S_k}\theta_i+\sum_{i=1}^I\left(\theta_i-a(\theta)\right)^+,\) (6)

where the second equality uses the identity _x_<sup>+</sup>=_x_+(-_x_)<sup>+</sup>. Lemma 1 says that expected mismatch loss is an upper bound on EOC and that for specific threshold functions it equals EOC.

LEMMA 1. _Let_ \(\theta^{(k)},\theta^{(k+1)}\) _denote the kth and_ (_k_+1)_th order statistics of_ \(\theta\) _respectively._

(_i)_ _For any threshold function a,_ \(\text{EOC}(S_k;p_{t-1})\le\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{M}(\theta;S_k,a)\big|p_{t-1}\big]\).<tbc>

_(ii)_ _If_ \(a(\theta)\in[\theta^{(k+1)},\theta^{(k)}]\) _almost surely, then_ \(\text{EOC}(S_k;p_{t-1})=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{M}(\theta;S_k,a)\big|p_{t-1}\big]\).

_Proof._ All proofs are provided in the Appendix.

Lemma 1 applies to an arbitrary state _p_<sub>_t_-1</sub> but does not involve future evaluations. Thus, its usefulness is in ensuring that, over the course of the evaluation rounds, if we conduct evaluations that make mismatch<tbc>

<tbc>loss small, then the resulting EOC will also be small. The bound holds with equality, for example, for the threshold \(a(\unknown)=\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{(k)}+\theta^{(k+1)})\). However, taking the expectation of mismatch loss is not tractable when the threshold is a function of such order statistics. We therefore restrict _a_ to a family of functions that allows for tractable analysis and find, within that family, the threshold function that gives the tightest bound on EOC.

The expected mismatch loss \(\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{M}(\unknown;S_k,a)|p_{t-1}]\) has terms of the form \(\mathbb{E}[(\theta_i-a(\unknown))^+|p_{t-1}]\). Since \(\unknown|p_{t-1}\) is Gaussian, the difference \(\theta_i-a(\unknown)\) is Gaussian whenever the threshold is affine in \(\unknown\), and the terms \(\mathbb{E}[(\theta_i-a(\unknown))^+|p_{t-1}]\) then have expressions amenable to analysis. This motivates the affine family of thresholds

\(a_{q,\mathbf{b}}(\unknown):=q+\mathbf{b}^\top(\unknown-\unknown_{t-1}),q\in\mathbb{R},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^I,\)

## 3.3. The surrogate loss

As discussed above, we treat the expected mismatch loss \(\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{M}(\theta;S_k^*(\mu_{t-1}),a_{q_t,b_t})|p_{t-1}]\) as a static objective fixed at state _p_<sub>_t_-1</sub> and use it to estimate how valuable each potential evaluation will be. We fix \(\mu_{t-1}\), \(S_k^*(\mu_{t-1})\), and (_q<sub>t</sub>,b<sub>t</sub>_) and value an evaluation (_i,j_) through the uncertainty it is expected to reduce. Accordingly, define its expected posterior covariance after evaluation (_i,j_)

\(\overline{\Sigma_t}((i,j),p_{t-1}):=\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}}\mathbb{P}(X_{ij}=x|p_{t-1})\text{Cov}\left(\theta|X_{ij}=x,p_{t-1}\right),\)

and \(\overline{p_t}(i,j):=N\left(\mu_{t-1},\overline{\Sigma_t}((i,j),p_{t-1})\right)\). We call <o>_p_</o><sub>t</sub>(_i,j_) the _expected posterior_, since both of its moments are the expected posterior moments: the expected covariance, and the mean by the martingale property<tbc>

of Bayesian updating. Then we define the surrogate loss associated with evaluation (_i,j_) as the expected mismatch loss, with expectation taken with respect to _p_t(_i,j_), \(\mathbb{E}_{\unknown\sim\overline{p_t}(i,j)}\big[\mathcal{M}\big(\unknown;S_k^*\big(\unknown_{t-1}\big),a_{q_t,\mathbf{b}_t}\big)\big].\) (8) In (8), the current prior and the threshold determine which items’ uncertainty is consequential, while \(\overline{\Sigma_t}((i,j),p_{t-1})\) determines how much of that uncertainty is expected to remain after evaluation (_i,j_). Lemma 2 gives an explicit expression for \(\overline{\Sigma_t}((i,j),p_{t-1})\). LEMMA 2. _Starting with prior_ \(N(\unknown_{t-1},\Sigma_{t-1})\)_, let_ \(\unknown_{t-1,0}:=\theta_0\) _and, for evaluation_ \((i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\)_, define_ \(\alpha_{t,ij}:=\frac{\beta_j(\mu_{t-1,i}-\mu_{t-1,j})}{\sqrt{1+\beta_j^2\sigma_{t-1,ij}^2}}\text{\textit{and}}\delta_{t,ij}:=\frac{\beta_j^2\sigma_{t-1,ij}^2}{1+\beta_j^2\sigma_{t-1,ij}^2}\frac{\phi(\alpha_{t,ij})^2}{\Phi(\alpha_{t,ij})\Phi(-\alpha_{t,ij})}.\) _Then the expected posterior covariance is_ \(\overline{\Sigma_t}((i,j),p_{t-1})=\Sigma_{t-1}-\frac{\delta_{t,ij}}{\sigma_{t-1,ij}^2}\Sigma_{t-1}(\mathbf{e}_i-\mathbf{e}_j)(\mathbf{e}_i-\mathbf{e}_j)^\top\Sigma_{t-1}.\) (9) Here \(\delta_{t,ij}\) is the expected proportion of the variance of \(\theta_i-\theta_j\) reduced by the evaluation. This depends on how uncertain the outcome is a priori, the variance of \(\theta_i-\theta_j\), and the evaluation accuracy. The covariance terms in (9) determine how the information learned about (_i,j_) indirectly affects our posterior about other items through correlation. Plugging in the expected covariance in (9), the surrogate loss in (8) is \(\mathbb{E}_{\unknown\sim\overline{p_t}(i,j)}\big[\mathcal{M}\big(\unknown;S_k^*\big(\unknown_{t-1}\big),a_{q_t,\mathbf{b}_t}\big)\big]=kq_t-\sum_{\ell\in S_k^*(\unknown_{t-1})}\mu_{t-1,\ell}+\sum_{\ell=1}^I\mathbb{E}_{\unknown\sim\overline{p_t}(i,j)}\big[(\theta_\ell-a_{q_t,\mathbf{b}_t}(\unknown))^+\big].\) On the right-hand side, only the last term depends on (_i,j_), which can be thought of as the controllable part of the surrogate loss. ## 4.1. Marginal scores

Consider an arbitrary round _t_ for which we write L((_i,j_)) and \(\mathcal{L}_\ell((i,j))\) for the losses in (10), leaving the dependence on _p_<sub>_t_-1</sub> implicit. Let \(\mathcal{L}(0)=\sum_{\ell=1}^I\mathcal{L}_\ell(0)\) be the loss before any evaluation, obtained by replacing \(\sigma'_{t,\ell}(i,j)\) and \(z'_{t,\ell}(i,j)\) with \(\sigma_{t-1,\ell}\) and \(z_{t-1,\ell}\). To choose what evaluation to conduct we compute the decrease in surrogate loss per unit of resource

\(\psi_{t,ij}:=\frac{\mathcal{L}(0)-\mathcal{L}((i,j))}{r_J}\)

for each evaluation, then evaluate \(\mathrm{argmax}_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}:r_j\le R_t}\psi_{t,ij}\). This procedure, Surrogate Allocation (SA), is given in Algorithm 1.

\(\psi_{t,ij}=\frac{\mathcal{L}(0)-\mathcal{L}((i,j))}{r_J}=\frac{1}{r_J}\sum_{\ell=1}^I\int_{(\sigma_{t,\ell}^\prime(i,j))^2}^{\sigma_{t-1,\ell}^2}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_\ell}{\partial v}dv=\frac{1}{r_J}\sum_{\ell=1}^I\int_0^{1-\frac{(\sigma_{t,\ell}^\prime(i,j))^2}{\sigma_{t-1,\ell}^2}}\frac{\sigma_{t-1,\ell}}{2\sqrt{1-s}}\phi\left(\frac{z_{t-1,\ell}}{\sqrt{1-s}}\right)ds.\) (11)

The upper limit in the integral corresponds to the proportion of item \(\ell\)’s uncertainty (relative to the threshold) reduced by conducting evaluation (_i,j_). To see this more clearly, by Lemma 2 we have

\(1-\frac{(\sigma_{t,\ell}^\prime(i,j))^2}{\sigma_{t-1,\ell}^2}=\delta_{t,ij}\mathrm{Corr}\big(\theta_i-\theta_j,\theta_\ell-a_{q_t,b_t}(\theta)\big)^2,\)

where \(\delta_{t,ij}\) is the expected proportion of the variance of \(\theta_i-\theta_j\) reduced by the evaluation. The squared term measures how much of the variance reduction of (_i,j_) transfers to item \(\ell\) through correlation.

The integrand measures how valuable it is to reduce item \(\ell\)’s uncertainty for our objective. It is the instantaneous decrease in expected mismatch loss per additional proportion of its variance removed. The \(\phi(z_{t-1,\ell})\) term is large when we are highly uncertain about which side of the top-_k_ threshold item \(\ell\) lies on, which occurs when either the mean \(\mu_{t-1,\ell}\) is close to the expected threshold level _q<sub>t</sub>_ or when \(\sigma_{t-1,\ell}\) is large. The additional standard deviation term \(\sigma_{t-1,\ell}\) scales this uncertainty by how far the item’s utility may be from the threshold, reflecting that selection mistakes are penalized by their magnitude.

Put together, (11) scores an evaluation by how much its uncertainty reduction impacts expected mismatch loss across all items. The integrand captures how valuable reducing item \(\ell\)’s uncertainty (relative to the threshold) is, and the upper limit of the integral captures how much of this item’s uncertainty is reduced by evaluating (_i,j_), either directly when \(\ell\in\{i,j\}\) or indirectly through correlation when \(\ell\notin\{i,j\}\).

## 4.2. The sequential procedure

Now that we have an algorithm to choose the next evaluation, we lay out the full sequential evaluation procedure in Algorithm 2. It takes a family of policies {EVALUATIONRULE<sup>_R<sub>t</sub>_</sup>} that map the state and budget to an affordable evaluation. For now, the evaluation rule can be thought of as SA, but we write it in general form as we will introduce a different evaluation rule for the endgame in §5. It also assumes the posterior update comes from a BELIEFUPDATE procedure implementing an approximate inference method from Approximation 1.

**Algorithm 2** Sequential procedure

**Input:** prior \((\mu_0,\Sigma_0)\), _R_, {EVALUATIONRULE<sup>_R<sub>t</sub>_</sup>}

1: \(t\leftarrow 1,R_1\leftarrow R\)

2: **while** \(R_t\ge min(r_0,r_1)\)

3: \((i_t,j_t)\leftarrow\text{EVALUATIONRULE}^{R_t}(\mu_{t-1},\Sigma_{t-1})\)

8: \(T\leftarrow t-1\)

## 4.3. Asymptotic consistency

A natural concern with a policy based on a static objective is that it may reach a state from which, even with an infinite remaining budget, some items outside the final top-_k_ choice retain a positive probability of belonging to the true top-_k_. We show that this can never be the case for Algorithm 2 with EVALUATIONRULE<sup>_R<sub>t</sub>_</sup> = SA: in particular, the algorithm is asymptotically consistent, meaning EOC \(\rightarrow 0\) as \(R\rightarrow\infty\), under two mild assumptions.

ASSUMPTION 1. _The true link function_ \(g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow(0,1)\) _is continuous, symmetric (g_(-_x)=_1-_g(x)), strictly increasing, and log-concave._

Assumption 1 is satisfied by the probit link we use \((g=\Phi)\) and allows for more general links.

ASSUMPTION 2. _Let_ \((\mu_t^*,\Sigma_t^*)\) _denote the exact first two moments of the posterior (which are generally unavailable in closed form). The approximate posterior moments_ \((\mu_t,\Sigma_t)\) _satisfy:_ (i) _there exist constants_ \(0<\chi_-\le\chi_+<\infty\) _such that, almost surely, for all sufficiently large t,_ \(\chi_-\Sigma_t^*\unknown\Sigma_t\unknown\chi_+\Sigma_t^*\), (ii) \(sup_t\|\mu_t\|_\infty<\infty\) _almost surely, and_ (iii) \(\mathbb{E}[\|\mu_T-\mu_T^*\|_\infty]\rightarrow 0\) _as_ \(R\rightarrow\infty\)_, where_ \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) _is the L-infinity norm._

Assumption 2 says that whatever method we use in the BELIEFUPDATE step eventually yields a "good" estimate of the first two moments of the true posterior given the collected data.

THEOREM 2. _Under Assumptions 1 and 2, Algorithm 2 with_ EVALUATIONRULE<sup>_R<sub>t</sub>_</sup>=SA _satisfies_

\(\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\in S_k^*(\theta)}\theta_i-\sum_{i\in S_k^*(\mu_T)}\theta_i\right]\rightarrow 0\text{\textit{as}}R\rightarrow\infty.\)

**5. The endgame**

Conceptually, the allocation rule in SA is compelling, particularly for early and middle rounds: even if it is not forward-looking in a dynamic sense, it values evaluations that are useful beyond their potential influence on this round’s posterior top-_k_ set. But near the end of the horizon, the value of such exploration is small, and in the last round it is zero. Hence, since the surrogate objective is not horizon-aware, this strength of SA can turn negative in _the endgame_. To "zoom in" on the items that are actual top-_k_ candidates in the endgame is precisely the nature of KG-type policies. We develop the KG policy for our problem in §5.1 and a rule for when to switch to it in §5.2.

**5.1. The sequential KG policy**

Recall from §2.3 that the KG policy chooses an evaluation

\((i_t,j_t)\in argmax_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}:r_j\le R_t}\psi_{t,ij}^\text{KG}\text{where}\psi_{t,ij}^\text{KG}:=\frac{V_\text{myopic}((i,j)|p_{t-1})}{r_j}.\)

To compute _V_myopic((_i,j_)|_p_<sub>_t_-1</sub>), whose expression is given in (4), Lemma 3 gives explicit expressions for the probability of each outcome of an evaluation and the resulting posterior means given the outcome.

LEMMA 3. _Starting with prior_ \(N(\mu_{t-1},\Sigma_{t-1})\)_, for evaluation_ \((i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\) _and outcome_ \(x\in\{-1,1\}\),

\(\mathbb{P}(X_{ij}=x|p_{t-1})=\Phi(x\alpha_{t,ij})\text{\textit{and}}\mu_t(x|(i,j))=\mu_{t-1}+\frac{x\beta_J\phi(x\alpha_{t,ij})}{\Phi(x\alpha_{t,ij})\sqrt{1+\beta_j^2\sigma_{t-1,ij}^2}}\Sigma_{t-1}(\mathbf{e}_i-\mathbf{e}_j),\)

_where_ \(\alpha_{t,ij}\) _is defined in Lemma 2._

As discussed in §2.3, when no outcome of any affordable evaluation can change the posterior top-_k_ set, all of the myopic gains \(\psi_{t,ij}^\text{KG}\) are zero. The KG policy then requires a fallback rule to determine which evaluation to conduct. Algorithm 3 gives the resulting KG procedure.

**Algorithm 3** Knowledge gradient (KG)

**Input:** \(\unknown_{t-1}\), \(\Sigma_{t-1}\), \(R_t\ge\mathrm{min}(r_0,r_1)\)

1: Compute \(\psi_{t,ij}^\mathrm{KG}\) for all \((i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\) with \(r_j\le R_t\)

2: \((i,j)\leftarrow\mathrm{argmax}_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}:r_j\le R_t}\psi_{t,ij}^\mathrm{KG}\)

3: **if** \(\psi_{t,ij}^\mathrm{KG}=0\)

4: Choose an affordable (_i,j_) using the fallback rule

5: **return** (_i,j_)

### 5.2. Endgame when?

Up to this point, Algorithm 2 provides the general sequential procedure, and we have given two algorithms for its EVALUATIONRULE: SA (Algorithm 1) and KG (Algorithm 3). What remains is a rule for when to use which. SA was designed for the bulk of the evaluation process and KG for the endgame, so we consider the following class of policies: run SA until a predetermined share \(\nu\) of the budget has been spent, then switch to KG.<sup>2</sup> We refer to \(\nu\) as the switching point. Within this class, we choose the switching point via Monte Carlo simulation. For \(\nu\in[0,1]\), let \(\pi_\nu\) denote the policy obtained from Algorithm 2 using EVALUATIONRULE<sup>_R<sub>t</sub>_</sup>= SA while \(R-R_t<\nu R\) and EVALUATIONRULE<sup>_R<sub>t</sub>_</sup>= KG once \(R-R_t\ge\nu R\), so that \(\pi_1\) is SA throughout and \(\pi_0\) is KG throughout. Given a problem specification \((I,k,R,r_0,r_1,p_0,\beta_0,\beta_1,\theta_0)\), let

\(\mathrm{EOC}\left(S_k^*(\unknown_T);\pi_\nu\right):=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\in S_k^*(\theta)}\theta_i-\sum_{i\in S_k^*(\unknown_T)}\theta_i\right|\pi_\nu\right],\)

where the expectation is over \(\theta\) with prior distribution _p_<sub>0</sub> and over the outcomes _X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>T</sub>_ drawn from the likelihood under policy \(\pi_\nu\).

We choose the switching point by a marginal analysis over a fixed set of candidate switching points \(0\le\nu_1<\nu_2<\cdots<\nu_J\le 1\). Let \(\widehat{\mathrm{EOC}}\left(S_k^*(\unknown_T);\pi_\nu\right)\) denote the Monte Carlo estimate of \(\mathrm{EOC}\left(S_k^*(\unknown_T);\pi_\nu\right)\), obtained by averaging the realized opportunity cost \(\sum_{i\in S_k^*(\theta)}\theta_i-\sum_{i\in S_k^*(\unknown_T)}\theta_i\) over _M_ independent simulated runs of \(\pi_\nu\), each drawing \(\theta\sim p_0\) and the outcomes from the specified likelihood. Starting from \(\nu_J\) (\(\nu_J=1\) meaning SA all the way through), we move the switching point back one candidate at a time, from \(\nu_h\) to \(\nu_{h-1}\) (peeling back the last stretch of SA into KG), as long as the marginal reduction \(\widehat{\mathrm{EOC}}\left(S_k^*(\unknown_T);\pi_{\nu_h}\right)-\widehat{\mathrm{EOC}}\left(S_k^*(\unknown_T);\pi_{\nu_{h-1}}\right)\) remains positive. We stop at the first \(\nu^*\) at which peeling back further fails to reduce \(\widehat{\mathrm{EOC}}\), and deploy the policy \(\pi_{\nu^*}\). We will refer to this as the switching procedure, and to our method, the policy \(\pi_{\nu^*}\), as SE (Surrogate to Endgame).

To conclude the analysis, we consider settings where evaluations are assigned in batches whose outcomes are observed at once before the next batch is chosen. While we have presented the problem sequentially, the model and analysis for the surrogate were developed with batching in mind, and extend naturally.

## 6.1. Surrogate batch construction

Choosing the batch that minimizes the surrogate loss in each round is an integer program that quickly becomes intractable as the batch budget grows. We therefore build a batch by committing to one evaluation at a time. The first evaluation is chosen as in the fully sequential problem, by maximizing the marginal decrease in surrogate loss per unit of resource from §4.1. However, unlike the sequential problem, we must choose subsequent evaluations before observing the outcomes of the evaluation already committed to the batch. If we continued to use the original marginal scores, we would value each evaluation as if it were the only one in the batch, allocating multiple evaluations to reduce the same uncertainty.

Consider the choice of the second evaluation. Suppose the first evaluation committed to the batch is (_i,j_). Although we have not yet observed its outcome, we can account for the information we expect to learn from it through its expected posterior covariance. By Lemma 2,

\(\overline{\Sigma_t}((i,j),p_{t-1})=\Sigma_{t-1}-\frac{\delta_{t,ij}}{\sigma_{t-1,ij}^2}\Sigma_{t-1}(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^\top\Sigma_{t-1}.\)

This covariance reflects the uncertainty expected to remain _after_ the first evaluation. To choose the second evaluation, we use this covariance in place of \(\Sigma_{t-1}\) and recompute the marginal scores from §4.1, keeping \(\mu_{t-1}\) and (_q<sub>t</sub>,b<sub>t</sub>_) fixed. Each candidate evaluation is scored by its _additional_ reduction in surrogate loss, accounting for the information we already expect to learn from the first. We choose the evaluation with the highest marginal score per unit of resource.

We next extend this approach to constructing an entire batch. The complication is that computing the expected posterior covariance after several committed evaluations requires taking the weighted average over their (many) possible joint outcomes. Instead, we approximate it by repeatedly applying the single-evaluation expected covariance update, using the updated expected covariance from the evaluations already committed.

Formally, let _n_ denote the matrix recording the evaluations committed so far in the batch, where _n<sub>ij</sub>_ corresponds to the number of evaluations of (_i,j_). Define _F<sup>ij</sup>_ as a matrix of the same size as _n_, with \(F_{ij}^{ij}=1\) and zero elsewhere. Let \(\Sigma'_t(n)\) denote our approximation of the expected posterior covariance, with \(\Sigma'_t(0)=\Sigma_{t-1}\). After adding evaluation (_i,j_) to the batch, it updates according to

\(\Sigma'_t(n+F^{ij})=\Sigma'_t(n)-\frac{\delta'_{t,ij}(n)}{(\sigma_{t,ij}^\prime(n))^2}\Sigma'_t(n)(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^\top\Sigma'_t(n),\) (12)

where \((\sigma_{t,ij}^\prime(n))^2\) and \(\delta'_{t,ij}(n)\) are computed as in Lemma 2, using \(\Sigma'_t(n)\) in place of \(\Sigma_{t-1}\).

Let \(\mathcal{L}(0;\Sigma'_t(n))\) be the surrogate loss before adding another evaluation and \(\mathcal{L}((i,j);\Sigma'_t(n))\) be the loss after adding (_i,j_). The marginal score of (_i,j_) is

\(\psi_{t,ij}(n)=\frac{\mathcal{L}(0;\Sigma'_t(n))-\mathcal{L}((i,j);\Sigma'_t(n))}{r_j}.\) (13)

Using these scores, the batch-building procedure is given in Algorithm 4. We consider elastic round budgets, meaning that as long as some budget remains in the current round, the algorithm may choose any evaluation provided it satisfies the total budget constraint. If its cost exceeds the remaining round budget, the excess is deducted from the next round’s budget. First, it optimizes over possible batch allocations, which we address through sequential batch construction, as in §6.1. Second, computing the myopic value of a given batch requires the outcome probabilities and posterior means for every possible combination of batch outcomes. We derive explicit expressions for these quantities given a batch outcome (analogous to Lemma 3), but they involve multivariate normal CDFs whose dimension grows with the batch size, making them expensive to evaluate numerically (Genz and Bretz 2009). Moreover, a batch of _U_ evaluations has 2_U_ possible outcomes, each requiring these calculations. The computational difficulty comes from considering all the ways the evaluations in a batch can jointly move the posterior means. We instead approximate the myopic value of a batch by decomposing it into the myopic values of sub-batches of at most _w_ evaluations. This retains interaction effects among up to _w_ evaluations while keeping the computation tractable: the value of each sub-batch requires normal CDFs of dimension at most _w_ and a sum over at most 2_w_ outcomes. _Configurations._ We consider \(I\in\{10,20,40,80,160\}\) and selection sizes \(k\in\{1,\sqrt{0.1I},0.1I\}\) (rounded). ## 8. Concluding remarks

For adaptive top-_k_ selection, we consider a unifying generative model for ratings (thumbs-up/down) and pairwise comparisons and allow the two input types to differ in both accuracy and cost. We replace the resulting intractable dynamic program with a novel surrogate-based allocation method. Despite consisting of a sequence of state-based static optimization problems, it is effectively forward-looking by rewarding decision-relevant uncertainty reduction. Based on the surrogate, we construct an allocation policy whose decision rule decomposes into interpretable parts that give insight into exactly why a particular evaluation was chosen. For the endgame regime, we switch to the knowledge gradient policy, with a criterion for when to do so, and extend the procedure to the batched evaluation setting. Finally, we show that our method performs well in simulations, stress-test the approximation made in the analysis, and test the method under model misspecification.

There are a number of exciting possible extensions for future work. One can consider heterogeneous evaluators whose \(\beta\)’s and \(\theta_0\) are unknown and learned from the evaluations. Additionally, one may consider richer evaluation types. Our model and analysis extend to ratings with any number of categories using an ordered probit model. However, considering partial rankings of a subset larger than two items would require additional work. ### A.1. Surrogate batch construction

Throughout the construction of a batch, we hold \(\mu_{t-1}\), \(S_k^*(\mu_{t-1})\), and (_q<sub>t</sub>,b<sub>t</sub>_) fixed, as in §3.3. For a candidate batch _n_, its expected posterior covariance is<tbc>

\(\overline{\Sigma_t}(n,p_{t-1}):=\mathbb{E}\big[\text{Cov}(\theta|p_t)\big|n,p_{t-1}\big].\)

<tbc>Here _p<sub>t</sub>_ denotes the posterior after observing the outcomes of _n_ and the expectation is over all possible outcomes of the batch. For a round budget _B<sub>t</sub>_, substituting this covariance into the surrogate gives the integer program

\(min_n\sum_{\ell=1}^I\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim N\left(\mu_{t-1},\overline{\Sigma_t}(n,p_{t-1})\right)}\big[\left(\theta_\ell-a_{q_t,b_t}(\theta)\right)^+\big]\text{s.t.}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}}r_jn_{ij}\le B_t,n_{ij}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\text{for all}(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}.\) (A.1)

As in (10), we have dropped the terms that do not depend on _n_. We approximately solve (A.1) by constructing the batch one evaluation at a time, as in Algorithm 4. To choose each additional evaluation, we approximate the expected posterior covariance in the objective by \(\Sigma'_t(n)\) using (12).

<tbc>Consider adding an evaluation (_i,j_) to _n_. If the outcomes of _n_ were observed, the resulting posterior _p<sub>t</sub>_ would give expected covariance \(\overline{\Sigma_t}((i,j),p_t)\) after the additional evaluation. Averaging over the outcomes of _n_ gives

\(\overline{\Sigma_t}(n+F^{ij},p_{t-1})=\mathbb{E}\big[\overline{\Sigma_t}((i,j),p_t)\big|n,p_{t-1}\big].\)

Here \(\overline{\Sigma_t}((i,j),p_t)\) averages over the two outcomes of (_i,j_) given _p<sub>t</sub>_, while the outer expectation averages over the outcomes of the already committed batch _n_.

We approximate this expectation by fixing the covariance after _n_ at \(\Sigma'_t(n)\). We then compute the expected covariance after adding (_i,j_) by averaging over its two possible outcomes under \(N(\mu_{t-1},\Sigma'_t(n))\), giving

\(\overline{\Sigma_t}(n+F^{ij},p_{t-1})\approx\overline{\Sigma_t}\big((i,j),N(\mu_{t-1},\Sigma'_t(n))\big)=\Sigma'_t(n+F^{ij}),\)

where the equality follows from Lemma 2 and gives (12). The first update is exact because _n_=0 and \(\Sigma'_t(0)=\Sigma_{t-1}\). Note that for the same batch matrix _n_, the approximation \(\Sigma'_t(n)\) can differ depending on the order in which evaluations are committed.

\(V_{myopic}(n|p_{t-1})=\sum_{H\subseteq\{1,\dots,U\}}\Gamma_H.\)

We next define the truncated approximation. For any integer \(w\ge 1\), define the order-_w_ truncation \(\widehat{V}_{\mathrm{myopic},w}(n|p_{t-1}):=\sum_{H\subseteq\{1,\dots,U\},|H|\le w}\Gamma_H\).

\(V_{myopic}(n|p_{t-1})-\widehat{V}_{myopic,w}(n|p_{t-1})=\sum_{H\subseteq\{1,\dots,U\},|H|\ge w+1}\Gamma_H.\)

If there are no interaction terms of higher order than _w_, i.e., if the batch size is at most _w_, then the approximation is exact. This truncation makes the value function tractable, while still allowing us to capture some of the interaction effects between evaluations in a batch. Every retained interaction term involves computing _V_<sub>myopic</sub> on sub-batches of size at most _w_, which requires sums over at most 2_<sup>w</sup>_ outcome vectors with multivariate normal CDFs of dimension at most _w_, regardless of the batch size _U_.

## D.2. Proof roadmap

There are two main components to the proof. The first, and far more technical, is to argue that the set of directions the algorithm samples infinitely many times contains the decision-relevant subspace \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\) in its span. The second component then argues that, if this is the case, the full history identifies \(P\theta\), and thus the expected opportunity cost decays to 0 as well.

To prove the first claim, we will argue by contradiction. Let \(E_\infty\) be the set of directions sampled infinitely often, and let \(M:=\mathrm{span}(E_\infty)\). We assume by contradiction that \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\unknown\in M\), and condition on an event \(\Omega_\mathcal{E}:=\{E_\infty=\mathcal{E}\}\), where the set of recurrent directions is fixed. On this event, after some finite random time, every subsequently sampled direction lies in E. This reduces the proof to showing two things: for the directions \(L\in\mathcal{E}\), their marginal score \(G_t(L)\rightarrow 0\), while the total score over D stays bounded away from 0. Thus, for all sufficiently large _t_, at least one direction outside E has a larger score than every direction in E, contradicting the assumption that every subsequently sampled direction lies in E.

The proof of Theorem 2 relies on eight lemmas, organized as follows. Lemma D.1 establishes that posterior variance goes to 0 and the posterior mean converges along every direction in the span of recurrently sampled directions. Lemma D.2 proves that posterior variance remains uniformly positive outside that span. Lemmas D.3 and D.4 transfer these conclusions to the approximate posterior covariance and provide the bounds needed for the marginal scores. Lemma D.5 bounds the affine threshold and the weights _w_<sub>_t_-1_,i_</sub>. Lemma D.6 shows that the scores of recurrent directions decay, while Lemma D.7 shows that the total score stays bounded away from 0 whenever \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\) is not contained in the recurrent span. Finally, Lemma D.8 shows that "projected" mean convergence suffices for expected opportunity cost.
